title: First light
brief: A 9 V battery, a 1 kΩ (1000 Ω) resistor and a red LED are on the Bench, wired except for the return from the LED's cathode (its bar end) to the battery's − terminal. Close the loop with one wire (W), then press Run (F5): it asks for your prediction of the LED's current before it runs. One loop: the same current flows through the battery, R1 and D1, so the LED's current is R1's, and a resistor's current is the voltage across it divided by its resistance. To read the current, press M until the meter's A tool is on, click D1's anode pin (the one on R1's side; the meter goes into the loop there), then click the socket marked mA (milliamps: 1 mA = 0.001 A) to put the red lead in it. Then submit the design.
debrief:
If you predicted 9 V / 1 kΩ = 9 mA, the meter said 7.11 mA. Where did the rest of the 9 V go? Put the meter across each part (M, V between): 1.887 V across the LED (D1), 7.11 V across the resistor (R1; 7.113 V, but from 6 V up the meter shows two decimals). 1.887 V + 7.113 V = 9.000 V: around a closed loop the voltages across the parts add up to the source.

A lit LED holds a nearly fixed voltage (its forward voltage), about 1.9 V for this red LED, so R1 gets only what is left: 7.113 V / 1 kΩ = 7.113 mA, not 9 mA. The meter's own 1 Ω mA shunt adds to the loop's 1 kΩ while it reads, lowering the current by about one part in a thousand, too little to change the display. At the cathode pin the same current reads −7.11 mA: it enters the black lead, and the sign says which way it flows through the meter.

7.11 mA means 7.11 thousandths of a coulomb of charge pass each second, about 4.4 × 10¹⁶ electrons: Charge and current, below, is about that.

details: Open: the return from the LED's cathode (its bar end) to the battery's − terminal. One wire closes it.
One loop: the same current flows through the battery, R1 and D1, so the LED's current is R1's.
A resistor's current is the voltage across it divided by its resistance.
